name: mushroom tagliatelle
instructions:
Two variants — variant A is the dairy version (cream cheese OR crème fraîche as the thickening/creaming agent, per the Chris Collins base recipe from Don't Go Bacon My Heart). Variant B is an experimental vegan version (blended miso paste + silken tofu) I haven't tested yet. Same technique otherwise; both use pan-fried mushrooms as the load-bearing flavor.

Why this recipe exists in the cookbook: it's a chance to make a creamy italian pasta that doesn't just use a splash of heavy cream — the cream cheese (variant A) or blended silken tofu (variant B) build a genuinely THICK creamy base, not just a rich splash.

=== VARIANT A — DAIRY (CREAM CHEESE OR CRÈME FRAÎCHE) ===

From Chris Collins / Don't Go Bacon My Heart, cream-cheese path. Crème fraîche is a valid substitute for the cream cheese (see notes).

SHIITAKE PREFERRED FOR THIS RECIPE (see notes) — but any mushroom works.

INGREDIENTS (serves 2):
- 7 oz / 200g tagliatelle (or fettuccine / linguine — any long-cut pasta)
- 7 oz / 200g mushrooms (shiitake preferred; chestnut / baby portobello / button all work), sliced
- 3.5 oz / 100g full-fat cream cheese (OR equivalent crème fraîche), taken out of the fridge 15 min before use
- 1/2 cup / 120ml chicken stock
- 1/4 cup / 20g freshly grated parmesan (NOT the pre-shredded packet stuff — it doesn't melt right)
- 2 tbsp unsalted butter
- 2 cloves garlic, finely diced
- 1/2 tsp finely diced fresh thyme (see notes on herb choice)
- salt and black pepper
- reserved pasta water

PROCEDURE:
1. Melt butter in a large pan over medium heat. Add the sliced mushrooms and toss to coat. Spread out so each slice contacts the pan — don't crowd (they'll steam instead of fry). Let them fry undisturbed until golden on the bottom.
2. Meanwhile, start the pasta in well-salted boiling water. DON'T DRAIN the pasta water — you'll need it later.
3. Flip the mushrooms; fry until golden on the other side. Season with salt and pepper. Push mushrooms to the outside of the pan; add garlic to the middle. Fry ~1 min until it just picks up color, then pour in the chicken stock. Simmer until reduced by about half.
4. Turn heat to LOW. Add the cream cheese (or crème fraîche). Stir until fully blended into the reduced stock — no cream-cheese blobs.
5. Stir in the fresh thyme.
6. Transfer the cooked pasta straight from the pot to the pan (tongs; carries a little cooking water). Toss to combine. Sprinkle in the parmesan and continue tossing until the sauce thickens and coats the pasta.
7. Splash in reserved pasta water to thin the sauce as needed. If you overshoot, keep tossing over low heat until it re-thickens.
8. Season to taste. Serve immediately — the sauce thickens fast on the plate.

=== VARIANT B — VEGAN (BLENDED MISO PASTE + SILKEN TOFU) — EXPERIMENTAL, UNTESTED ===

Haven't tried this yet. The idea: replace the cream cheese with a blended base of silken tofu + light miso paste, run through a food processor until smooth. Everything else (mushrooms, garlic, thyme, pasta water, technique) stays the same.

RATIONALE: silken tofu blended smooth gives you the creamy body a cream-cheese sauce provides; miso adds the fermented-tangy depth that cream cheese contributes (cream cheese IS a fermented dairy — silken-tofu-plus-miso approximates the flavor axis, not just the texture). Use the food processor rule from spinach-ricotta (variant B in that recipe) — this whole application uses the same blended-vegan-cheese principle.

Use chicken stock alternative: vegetable stock or mushroom stock for the vegan version.

Both variants of this recipe want FRESH HERBS — see notes.
notes:
Source: Chris Collins, Don't Go Bacon My Heart — the mushroom tagliatelle recipe. Variant A captured as written; variant B is my untested extension.

=== SHIITAKE OR OYSTER — THE ONLY MUSHROOMS THAT WORK WELL HERE ===

Author says most mushroom varieties work, but in practice I've landed narrower: SHIITAKE or OYSTER are the only ones I can think of that work well in this dish. Either is a good pick. Others (chestnut / baby portobello / cremini / button) don't land as well against the cream-cheese-and-thyme axis — moved out of the recommended list.

=== PAN-FRIED MUSHROOMS ARE THE LOAD-BEARING FLAVOR — DON'T CROWD THE PAN ===

Pan-fried mushrooms are the whole savory backbone of both variants. Author's tips (all worth following):
- DON'T WASH THEM: damp cloth to clean. Water adds moisture and steams the fry.
- SPACE THEM OUT: don't cram, they'll steam not fry. Golden-brown surface is the goal.
- DON'T SALT AT THE START: salt draws out moisture. Season AFTER they're golden.
- GARLIC LATER, NOT AT THE START: fry mushrooms first, then push to the side and add garlic briefly.

=== MY REFINED VARIANT A APPROACH (AUG 22 2026) — SUCCESSFUL COOK ===

Refined version of variant A that worked well. Meaningful departures from the Chris Collins base recipe — logged here as the going-forward approach.

KEY MOVES:

1. OLIVE OIL INSTEAD OF BUTTER. Butter + cream cheese together is too heavy. Olive oil for the mushroom fry keeps the fat load balanced against the cream cheese base.

2. LOOSEN THE CREAM CHEESE WITH HOT WATER FIRST, 1 TSP AT A TIME. Best way I've found to make a cream cheese sauce: whisk in 1 tsp of HOT water at a time into the cream cheese, building up to a loose, pourable sauce texture before it ever touches the pan. Prevents cream-cheese blobs in the final pan; the sauce integrates cleanly.

3. POTATO STARCH IN THE CREAM CHEESE TO STABILIZE. Whisk a good amount of POTATO STARCH into the loosened cream cheese. The starch is what lets the sauce hold together when it hits the hot pan — the water burns off perfectly and you get a stable creamy sauce rather than a broken one. This is load-bearing for the whole technique.

4. CHICKEN STOCK IS BACK IN — BUT DON'T JUDGE THE SAUCE BEFORE PASTA + PASTA WATER GO IN. Earlier note said to skip the stock; walked back. The stock DOES help. Why the earlier confusion: when the mushroom sauce is 'born' in the pan (just cream cheese base + adds, no pasta yet), the stock tastes like too much — the cream cheese is concentrated at that stage and the stock over-salts / over-savory-loads it. But once you add pasta water + pasta, the cream dilutes and the stock lands correctly. Rule: don't season the pan sauce to taste on its own; wait until the pasta is in and tossed before making seasoning judgments.

5. OPTIONAL FLAVOR ADDS ALONGSIDE THE STOCK: PORCINI POWDER + RED CHILI FLAKES. Porcini reinforces the mushroom axis; red chili flakes add background heat. Both secondary — nice but not load-bearing. NOTE: fennel powder was in this stack in earlier notes; walked back — it clashes in this dish. Skip it.

6. WHITE WINE VINEGAR — NOT HARMFUL BUT UNNECESSARY: originally logged as part of the flavor stack; walked back. Vinegar didn't harm the sauce but it wasn't doing needed work either. Skip it. The starch-stabilized cream cheese base + porcini + fennel + chili flakes lands correctly without an added acid.

WANT TO TRY NEXT — WHITE WINE DEGLAZE ON THE MUSHROOMS (MIGHT WORK): instead of vinegar, deglaze the mushrooms in white wine before adding the cream cheese base. Might work — the starch stabilization should keep the sauce together against the wine acid, and wine's flavor character has more to offer than vinegar's brightness alone. Untested.

=== CREAM CHEESE vs CRÈME FRAÎCHE (VARIANT A) ===

Author's default is cream cheese — the cheese aspect mellows out significantly as the sauce comes together, and cream cheese gives you a thicker, more cohesive sauce than a splash of heavy cream would. This is the whole point of the recipe: a creamy italian pasta that's actually THICK-creamy rather than just cream-enriched.

CRÈME FRAÎCHE IS A VALID SUB: crème fraîche is thinner than cream cheese but has a similar cultured-dairy tang. Works if you don't have cream cheese or want a slightly less thick sauce. Same amount (~100g).

Both need to be at ROOM TEMP before adding — cold from the fridge won't blend smoothly into the reduced stock.

=== THE POINT — CREAMY ITALIAN PASTA WITHOUT JUST A SPLASH OF CREAM ===

Most creamy italian pastas cheat via a splash of heavy cream added at the end. This recipe builds actual body via the cream cheese (or crème fraîche) melted into the reduced stock — you get a THICK, cohesive sauce that clings to the pasta properly. The cream-cheese path is what makes it a genuinely creamy dish rather than a cream-enriched one.

Variant B (silken tofu + miso, blended) is the vegan analog of the same principle: build actual sauce body, don't just splash something creamy at the end.

=== FRESH HERBS — THYME + BASIL WELCOME IN BOTH VARIANTS ===

Both variants want fresh herbs — thyme is the author's default for the dairy version and it's the load-bearing herb here. FRESH BASIL also welcome in both variants (author's recipe doesn't call for it but it pairs cleanly with the mushroom + cream base).

Herb quantity: 1/2 tsp fresh thyme per author. Basil more generous — a torn handful at the end.

=== HERB SUBS (AUTHOR'S NOTES) ===

- TARRAGON: works at the same 1/2 tsp quantity as thyme. Stronger, more distinctive flavor — only sub if you like tarragon.
- PARSLEY: milder. Can use up to 2 tsp.
- FRESH ONLY: dried thyme / tarragon / parsley all read wrong here. Fresh matters.

=== FRESHLY GRATED PARMESAN, NOT PRE-SHREDDED ===

Author is emphatic: use freshly grated parmesan. Pre-shredded packet stuff doesn't melt properly — has anti-caking additives that mess with the sauce texture. This applies to variant A specifically (variant B doesn't use parmesan; use nutritional yeast alongside the miso or just skip).

=== PASTA WATER TO EMULSIFY THE SAUCE ===

Don't drain the pasta water — reserve a cup. Add splashes to the sauce as you toss with pasta; the starch emulsifies the fats into a smooth glossy sauce. If you overshoot (too watery), keep tossing over low heat and it re-thickens. If you undershoot (too thick), add more.

=== VARIANT B — EXPERIMENTAL, UNTESTED ===

Haven't tried variant B yet. The mental model: substitute the cream cheese slot with blended silken tofu + miso paste (both go in the food processor and get smoothed into a paste before adding to the pan). The tofu provides body, the miso provides fermented-tang and cheesy-ish depth.

Specific quantities untested — probably ~100g silken tofu + 1-2 tsp light miso to start, blend, taste, adjust.

Use vegetable stock or mushroom stock (not chicken stock) for the vegan version.

Same food processor rules apply as in spinach-ricotta variant B: not a blender (Nickelodeon slime problem doesn't apply here since there's no spinach, but the over-smoothing texture problem still does).

=== SEEDS — SUNFLOWER CONFIRMED (TOAST NEXT TIME); SESAME JURY-OUT; PUMPKIN UNTESTED ===

- SUNFLOWER SEEDS: worked well in the Aug 22 2026 cook. NEXT ATTEMPT — TOAST THEM FIRST. Adds depth against the mushroom + cream cheese base.
- SESAME SEEDS: jury is still out. Tried, but haven't landed on whether they work here.
- PUMPKIN SEEDS: untested. Log when tried.

=== WHITE WINE — STILL WANT TO TRY (MIGHT WORK); WHITE WINE VINEGAR WALKED BACK ===

White wine deglaze on the mushrooms is still a want-to-try — untested. Might work with the starch-stabilized cream cheese base (starch should protect against the wine acid).

WHITE WINE VINEGAR — TRIED, WALKED BACK: added in the Aug 22 2026 cook. Not harmful, but unnecessary — didn't do needed work. Skip it going forward.

=== SERVING ===

Serve immediately — the sauce thickens fast once it hits a plate. Author recommends garlic bread on the side. Any long-cut pasta (tagliatelle, fettuccine, linguine) works — long strands catch and hold the thick sauce; short pasta reads wrong here.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- spinach-ricotta: uses the same variant A/B dairy-vs-vegan-blend structure. Variant B here (silken tofu + miso blend) uses the same underlying vegan-savory technique as spinach-ricotta variant B (cashews + tofu + miso + nutritional yeast).
- master-italian-tomato-sauce-and-pesto: the tomato pasta sauce family. This recipe is the cream-based creamy analog — different register, similar 'pasta with a real sauce not just a splash' philosophy.
- pasta-ai-funghi: another mushroom pasta (if in this cookbook). Cross-reference if applicable.
